source.version: Published journal article, Rupkatha Journal 16(3), 2024; first published 27 October 2024 (PDF p. 1); complete local PDF and markdown conversion read.
source.title_on_document: Human Creativity Vs. Artificial Intelligence: A Comparison of Horror Fiction Crafting from ‘Bookish Minds Club’ at Souk Ahras University and Claude AI

paper_design_summary: Sixty student members of the Bookish Minds club at Souk Ahras University were divided evenly between Claude-assisted and unassisted horror-story writing, using identical prompts during three ordinary club sessions (p. 1, Abstract; pp. 5-7, sections 3.1-3.3). The paper calls this a controlled between-subjects experiment but does not state how students were allocated to groups (pp. 5-6, sections 3 and 3.2). Stories were scored on originality, atmosphere, tension build-up, and character depth using a 1-to-5 rubric; the scoring method and evaluator identities are not specified, so outcome measure is null (pp. 7-12, section 4).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were divided between G1 (Claude AI assistance) and G2 (writing without AI); the allocation mechanism is not stated.
assignment.quote: The participants were divided into two groups to evaluate the role of AI assistance versus human creativity in crafting horror fiction.
assignment.locator: p. 6, section 3.2 Intervention; p. 5, section 3 Methodology (between-subjects design); p. 1, Abstract (even division).

arms.name: G1: Claude AI-assisted writing
arms.description: Participants trained with Claude AI and used it to generate ideas, structure narratives, and refine stories; they integrated its suggestions into their writing (pp. 6-7, sections 3.2-3.3). The abstract states that the reported sample of 60 club members was divided evenly into two groups; final arm-specific analyzed participant counts are not stated (p. 1, Abstract; p. 9, section 4).

arms.name: G2: Unassisted writing
arms.description: Participants relied on their own creativity and writing skills without AI (pp. 6-7, sections 3.2-3.3). The abstract states that the reported sample of 60 club members was divided evenly into two groups; final arm-specific analyzed participant counts are not stated (p. 1, Abstract; p. 9, section 4).

participants.who: The reported study sample comprised 60 students from Souk Ahras University, including third-year bachelor (L3), Master One, and Master Two students, all active Bookish Minds reading-club members (pp. 5-6, section 3.1). The abstract states that they were divided evenly between the two groups (p. 1). The final number of people whose outputs entered the results is not stated, either overall or by arm; no participant flow or exclusions are reported (pp. 5-12, sections 3-4.1).
participants.quote: Sixty club members were divided evenly, with each group receiving identical horror fiction prompts to craft their stories.
participants.locator: p. 1, Abstract (60 club members divided evenly); pp. 5-6, section 3.1 Participants (60 students and their educational levels); p. 9, section 4 Results (group mean scores).

ai_tool.name_model: Claude AI; model version not stated
ai_tool.how_used: G1 trained with Claude, entered the supplied story prompts, captured full AI replies in screenshots, and integrated AI suggestions into handwritten drafts; assistance included generating ideas, structuring narratives, and refining stories (pp. 6-7, sections 3.2-3.3).

task.description: Craft short horror stories from identical prompts about a shadowy bedside figure, a creepy doll, and a forest with mysterious whispers; a distinct story was written in each club session (p. 1, Abstract; p. 6, section 3.3 Materials).
task.duration: Three ordinary club sessions, each 50 minutes (p. 6, section 3.3 Materials).

outcomes.name: Originality (Fear of the Unknown)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Scored with a 1-to-5 rubric; evaluator identities and the scoring procedure beyond the rubric are not stated (pp. 7-9, section 4). The scored stories were produced with Claude available to G1 during the club sessions and collected at session end (pp. 6-7, section 3.3); no later unassisted test is reported.

contrasts.reported: Reported ranges of mean originality scores across the three stories: Claude AI-assisted G1, 1.95 to 2.30; unassisted G2, 4.35 to 4.75. Ratings use a 1-to-5 rubric. These are ranges of reported scores, not confidence intervals; no SD, SE, or inferential comparison is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, section 4.1 Discussion of the Results, Originality (Fear of the Unknown); p. 7, section 4 Results (rubric); p. 9, section 4 Results (group means across stories).

outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: Reported score ranges across the three stories: Claude AI-assisted G1, 2.40 to 2.60; unassisted G2, 3.65 to 4.00. Ratings use a 1-to-5 rubric for the effectiveness of descriptive language and setting. These are ranges of reported scores, not confidence intervals; no SD, SE, or inferential comparison is reported.

outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Scored with a 1-to-5 rubric; evaluator identities and the scoring procedure beyond the rubric are not stated (pp. 7-9, section 4). The scored stories were produced with Claude available to G1 during the club sessions and collected at session end (pp. 6-7, section 3.3); no later unassisted test is reported.

contrasts.reported: Reported score ranges across the three stories: Claude AI-assisted G1, 3.95 to 4.30; unassisted G2, 2.45 to 2.60. Ratings use a 1-to-5 rubric for pacing and suspense. These are ranges of reported scores, not confidence intervals; no SD, SE, or inferential comparison is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 12, section 4.1, Tension Build-up (Pacing & Suspense); pp. 7-8, section 4 Results (rubric); p. 9, section 4 Results (group means across stories).

outcomes.name: Character Depth (Relatable Characters & Fears)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Scored with a 1-to-5 rubric; evaluator identities and the scoring procedure beyond the rubric are not stated (pp. 7-9, section 4). The scored stories were produced with Claude available to G1 during the club sessions and collected at session end (pp. 6-7, section 3.3); no later unassisted test is reported.

contrasts.reported: Reported score ranges across the three stories: Claude AI-assisted G1, 3.55 to 4.10; unassisted G2, 2.45 to 3.95. Ratings use a 1-to-5 rubric for character development, relatable fears, and motivations. The prose says Claude scores higher, but Figures 2 and 6 show higher AI scores for Stories 1 and 2 and a lower AI score for Story 3, so the direction across stories is mixed. These are ranges of reported scores, not confidence intervals; no SD, SE, or inferential comparison is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 12, section 4.1, Character Depth (Relatable Characters & Fears) and Figure 6; p. 10, Figure 2; pp. 7-8, section 4 Results (rubric); p. 9, section 4 Results (group mean scores).

eligibility.reason: Allocation is described only as division into two groups; neither random assignment nor a specific non-random allocation mechanism is reported (p. 6, section 3.2; p. 1, Abstract). The reported study sample is 60 students (pp. 5-6, section 3.1), but the paper does not state the final participant analysis denominator overall or by arm (p. 9, section 4; pp. 10-12, section 4.1); criterion 2 is therefore unclear under the analyzed-people threshold. Originality, atmosphere, tension build-up, and character depth are scored on the stories with a 1-to-5 rubric (pp. 7-9, section 4; pp. 10-12, Figures 2-6), meeting criterion 3. With criteria 1 and 2 unclear, core remains unclear; design_class remains other and context_class none because neither random nor non-random assignment is established.

one_line_finding: Claude-assisted stories scored lower on originality than unassisted stories (1.95-2.30 versus 4.35-4.75; p. 10, section 4.1) but higher on tension build-up (3.95-4.30 versus 2.45-2.60; p. 12, section 4.1), with the group-allocation method unstated (p. 6, section 3.2).
